chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Muhammad from Mu'alla ibn Muhammad from Muhammad ibn Jumhur from Ahmad ibn Hamza from Al-Husayn ibn al-Mukhtar from Abu Baseer who said:
Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) said: 'Mix with them with outwardly (apparent) and oppose them inwardly (hidden) when the ruler is childish'.

key_terms.الْإِمْرَةُ: The rulership or command; the political authority.
key_terms.الْبَرَّانِيَّةُ: Outwardly; the external, apparent aspect of behavior or appearance.
key_terms.الْجَوَّانِيَّةُ: Inwardly; the internal, hidden aspect of belief or state.
key_terms.صِبْيَانِيَّةٌ: Childishness; immaturity or lack of full maturity, often implying weakness or foolishness in leadership.

ai.seo_question: What is the Shia concept of mixing outwardly while opposing inwardly in times of weak leadership?
ai.summary: Imam Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) instructs the Shia to practice dissimulation (taqiyya) by maintaining outward conformity with the ruling authority while keeping their true beliefs hidden internally. This strategy is specifically recommended when the political leadership is characterized by immaturity or weakness ('childishness'), allowing the community to preserve its identity and avoid persecution. In Shia jurisprudence, this hadith is often cited to justify the flexibility of external actions (al-baraniyyah) versus internal conviction (al-jawwaniyyah), ensuring survival during periods of political instability or weak governance.
